title: Pricing by hours per project for Irrigation servicing
audience: Owners and technicians who write servicing quotes for irrigation systems and need a price that covers cost and earns a margin.
learningOutcomes: Calculate a cost per productive hour from the owner's own figures
Estimate servicing hours for a system, including zone runs, reporting, travel and checking time
Build a servicing quote from hours, a rate and a margin, and state its basis and exclusions

instruction.heading: Why hours are the starting unit
instruction.body: A servicing visit is a set of checks with a known sequence: access, controller, each zone, the report and travel. Hours make the cost of each check visible, so you can see what a seasonal check earns and what extra zones or faults cost to deal with. A flat price for a check hides the zone count, the fault rate and the travel, and it cannot be defended when a client asks why a visit costs what it does.

instruction.heading: Build the cost per productive hour
instruction.body: Divide the year's total cost of running the service business by its chargeable hours. Include wages with on-costs such as leave and superannuation (business.gov.au, updated 1 October 2026), the vehicle, the test equipment and its upkeep, insurance, any registration fees that apply to your work, software, administration and premises. Use chargeable hours, not paid hours. Confirm the award or agreement for each worker before using any wage figure, because pay rates are not stated in this lesson.

instruction.heading: Estimate the hours
instruction.body: Break each visit into access, controller check, zone runs, fault notes, the written report, travel and set-up. Estimate each zone run at a standard time from your own log, and add the report and travel as named lines. Add a set allowance for delay, such as a controller that needs a reset. Xero suggests 10 to 20 per cent for unexpected work (Xero Australia, 3 September 2026); set your own from your records. Compare quoted and actual time after each visit (Carters Trade Leader, 1 October 2025; New Zealand source, method only).

instruction.heading: Turn hours into a price
instruction.body: Multiply the crew hours by the cost per productive hour, add a margin for risk, such as an old controller or restricted site access, and apply the minimum charge. Any repair found during the visit is quoted separately after the check. Do not use the installation prices in the Melbourne cost guide as a benchmark for servicing: they are installation figures (What's the Damage, verified 1 November 2026).

instruction.heading: Keep the quote honest
instruction.body: The quote states the scope (zones, controller, report), the time basis, the exclusions (repairs outside the agreed list, supply problems, backflow testing), what the client provides (access, meter, controller), the watering window used for test runs, GST status and validity. Record every change to the scope and re-quote before any extra work starts (WA Consumer Protection, 4 September 2026).

instruction.heading: Review your estimates
instruction.body: Compare estimated and actual time for at least the first ten visits of each type. Change the standard time, the margin or the scope rules if the variance stays above your threshold. Review prices about every three months (Business Victoria, undated).

procedure: Gather the year's total business costs and the productive hours achieved in the same period.
Divide total costs by productive hours to get the cost per productive hour.
Break each servicing visit into access, controller, zone runs, reporting and travel, and estimate each as a range.
Add set-up, report writing and travel time as named lines.
Multiply the crew hours by the cost per productive hour, add the delay allowance, then apply the margin.
Apply the materials policy and the minimum charge, and quote any repair separately.
Write the quote with scope, hours basis, exclusions, client inputs, the watering window, GST status and validity.
Record actual hours after each visit and compare them with the estimate.

workedExamples.situation: Illustrative figures only, not market rates. A seasonal check of a six-zone system needs 1.5 crew-hours for the zone runs and checks, 0.5 hours for the written report, and 0.5 hours of travel and set-up. The owner's cost per productive hour is $60 (illustrative). The target margin on price is 25 per cent (illustrative).
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the cost of the visit, what is the price with a 25 per cent margin, and what changes if a 10 per cent delay allowance is added?
workedExamples.reasoning: The crew-hours total 2.5, so the cost is 2.5 multiplied by $60, which is $150. A 25 per cent margin on price means the price is $150 divided by 0.75, which is $200. With a 10 per cent delay allowance, the hours become 2.75 and the cost $165, so the price becomes $220. The allowance is billed only if the quote's terms say so. A repair found during the visit is quoted separately and does not change this price. The owner also plans the visit inside the watering window the client's address requires. Whether a test run counts as watering is not confirmed in this lesson, so the owner checks with the water authority first.

equipmentAndPpe: Time log for each visit, with estimated and actual columns

commonErrors.error: Pricing from the hourly wage alone
commonErrors.prevention: Include on-costs, vehicle, test equipment, insurance, registration and administration in the cost per productive hour.

commonErrors.error: Counting paid hours as productive hours
commonErrors.prevention: Use chargeable hours only when calculating the cost per productive hour.

commonErrors.error: Leaving out travel, report writing and checking time
commonErrors.prevention: Add these as named lines on every estimate.
List what is excluded, what the client provides, and the access and watering assumptions.

commonErrors.error: Never comparing estimates with actual hours
commonErrors.prevention: Record actual hours after each visit and review the variance monthly.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Pricing guidance only. The Australian Consumer Law applies to pricing statements, and misleading statements about prices are prohibited (ACCC, 15 July 2026). State and territory fair trading rules also apply and differ, so check the rules for your state.
Pay rates, allowances and on-costs may be set by an award or enterprise agreement. Check which one applies to each worker before using any cost figure. This lesson does not state those rates.

This lesson does not grant any registration or licence. Where a servicing visit includes regulated plumbing work, the registration that applies in that state must be held before the work is priced. NSW irrigation licensing is not confirmed.

qualityStandard: Each quote shows scope, hours or price basis, exclusions, client inputs, GST status and validity.
The cost per productive hour is calculated from the owner's own records and dated.
Actual hours are recorded for at least the first ten visits of each type and compared with the estimate.
No quote is issued without a margin decision and a minimum-charge check.
documentationEvidence: Cost per productive hour worksheet, dated, with the source of each figure
Quote showing scope, hours basis, exclusions, GST status and validity
Visit time log with estimated and actual hours
summary: Hours make the work visible, so start every servicing quote from hours.
Cost per productive hour uses chargeable time, not paid time.
Report writing, travel and checking time are named lines, and repairs are quoted separately.
Compare estimates with actual hours, and change the method when they diverge.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which costs belong in the cost per productive hour?
options: Only the hourly wage of the lowest-paid worker and nothing else from the accounts or the rent
The price the client pays, plus the deposit, the late fee and the crew bonus paid
The average hourly rate of competitors in the local area and their fees for the whole year
Wages with on-costs, vehicle, equipment, consumables, insurance and administration, divided by chargeable hours

knowledgeChecks.question: A servicing visit is estimated at 5 crew-hours and takes 8. What is the right response?
options: Record the actual hours, find the cause, and adjust the estimate and future quotes
Leave the estimate, since the client has already paid and the crew has finished
Reduce paid hours for the crew on the next job and skip the morning break
Raise the price for this client's next job only and no one else is charged more

knowledgeChecks.question: Why does a servicing quote need an exclusions list?
options: To hide the margin from the client and to keep the rates a secret from the crew
To make the quote longer and to fill up the page with more text and words for the client
To show what the price covers, so scope changes can be priced and disputes are reduced
To lower the client's expectations and to make the job seem much smaller than it is

sourceReferences: business.gov.au, 'Choose a pricing strategy', https://business.gov.au/products-and-services/choose-a-pricing-strategy, page metadata dated 1 October 2026. Supports: on-costs such as super, leave and tax belong in the hourly cost.
ACCC, 'Setting prices: what's allowed', https://www.accc.gov.au/business/pricing/setting-prices-whats-allowed, last modified 15 July 2026. Supports: misleading price statements are prohibited.

Xero Australia, 'How to price services', https://www.xero.com/au/guides/how-to-price-services/, dated 3 September 2026. Supports: divide by billable hours, not total hours; 10 to 20 per cent allowance for unexpected work; review prices at least once a year.

Carters Trade Leader, 'Estimating how many hours a job will take: Why 83% get it wrong', https://tradeleader.carters.co.nz/trade-skills/estimating-how-many-hours-a-job-will-take-why-83-get-it-wrong/, dated 1 October 2025. New Zealand publisher; general method only. Supports: compare quoted and actual labour.

What's the Damage, 'Landscaping cost Melbourne', https://whatsthedamage.com.au/landscaping-cost-melbourne/, verified 1 November 2026. Cost guide; not a regulator. Supports: installation figures, which are not used as a servicing price.

Business Victoria, 'Develop a pricing strategy', https://business.vic.gov.au/business-information/finance/pricing-for-profit/develop-a-pricing-strategy, no date shown. Supports: include total overheads and sales costs when checking a price; review about every three months.

WA Consumer Protection, 'Estimates, quotes and deposits', https://www.consumerprotection.wa.gov.au/estimates-quotes-and-deposits, last updated 4 September 2026. Western Australia only. Supports: record changes before extra work; total including GST.
